## Introduction

In the last three tutorials you read a real `devcontainer.json`, a real Dockerfile, and the workflow that turns that Dockerfile into a published image. Now you build the whole chain yourself, in miniature: a repo called `your-starter` that you can launch a Codespace from --- your own `codespace-starter`, without the teaching material you no longer need.

"Miniature" means one base image, one extra R package, one extension, and three settings. But every piece is real, and the shape is identical to the PPBDS version: a Dockerfile describes the image, a GitHub Actions workflow builds and publishes it, and a `devcontainer.json` pins it by exact version.

You never run `docker` yourself. A machine does, exactly as in the previous tutorial. And you keep this repo. Every other tutorial repo was disposable. This one is a tool you will use.

Everything you make in this tutorial --- the Dockerfile, the workflow, the `devcontainer.json` --- lives inside this repo. At the end you will turn it into a **template** so new projects can start from it with one click.

## Your Starter

The pieces are built in the order they depend on each other: the Dockerfile first, then the workflow that builds it, then the `devcontainer.json` that uses the result.

### Exercise 1

In the bash Terminal, at the top level of your `your-starter` repo, create a file called `Dockerfile` (no extension) with exactly this content:

```dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/rocker-org/devcontainer/tidyverse:4.5

# One package of your own, so this is provably YOUR image.
RUN R -q -e 'install.packages("praise")'

# Smoke test: fail the build if the package did not install.
RUN R -q -e 'stopifnot(requireNamespace("praise"))'
```

Then run `cat Dockerfile`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: your-starter-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "In the bash Terminal, at the top level of your your-starter repo, create a file called Dockerfile (no extension) with exactly this content: a FROM line for ghcr.io/rocker-org/devcontainer/tidyverse:4.5; a RUN line that installs one package of your own, so this is provably your image (R -q -e 'install.packages(\"praise\")'); and a RUN line that is a smoke test, failing the build if the package did not install (R -q -e 'stopifnot(requireNamespace(\"praise\"))'). Then run cat Dockerfile. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
your-starter $ cat Dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/rocker-org/devcontainer/tidyverse:4.5

# One package of your own, so this is provably YOUR image.
RUN R -q -e 'install.packages("praise")'

# Smoke test: fail the build if the package did not install.
RUN R -q -e 'stopifnot(requireNamespace("praise"))'
```

###

The `FROM` line starts from the same Rocker family as the PPBDS image, but at `:4.5`, not `:4.6`. R 4.6 changed how R starts up in a way that breaks the R extension's plot pane unless the image patches around it. The PPBDS Dockerfile carries such a patch, the `.First` shim near its arf section. Starting one version back sidesteps the problem. Pinning by tag rather than by digest is fine for a first version. The digest is the upgrade you read about in the previous tutorial.

The two `RUN` lines are the PPBDS discipline in miniature: install something, then **test** that it installed, so a broken build fails loudly instead of shipping a broken image.

### Exercise 2

Now the workflow. Create the folders and file `.github/workflows/build.yml` with this content, **replacing `YOUR_USERNAME` with your GitHub username in lowercase** (registry names must be lowercase):

```yaml
name: build-and-push

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ['v*']

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v6
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/YOUR_USERNAME/your-starter
          tags: |
            type=raw,value=latest,enable={{is_default_branch}}
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
```

Run `cat .github/workflows/build.yml`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: your-starter-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Now the workflow. Create the folders and file .github/workflows/build.yml with this content, replacing YOUR_USERNAME with your GitHub username in lowercase (registry names must be lowercase): a workflow named build-and-push that runs on pushes to main and on tags matching v*, with one job, build, on ubuntu-latest, with permissions contents: read and packages: write, whose steps check out the repo (actions/checkout@v5), set up buildx (docker/setup-buildx-action@v4), log in to the ghcr.io registry (docker/login-action@v4, username github.actor, password secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN), compute tags with docker/metadata-action@v6 (id meta) for images ghcr.io/YOUR_USERNAME/your-starter (type=raw latest enabled on the default branch, plus type=semver pattern version), and build and push with docker/build-push-action@v7 (context ., push true, tags from steps.meta.outputs.tags). Run cat .github/workflows/build.yml. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
your-starter $ cat .github/workflows/build.yml
name: build-and-push

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ['v*']
```

###

This is a shortened copy of the workflow you read in the previous tutorial: the same actions at the same versions, minus the caching. It checks out your repo, logs in to GHCR with the temporary `GITHUB_TOKEN` (which is what `permissions: packages: write` allows), computes the image tags, then builds and pushes. There are two triggers. Every push to `main` refreshes `latest`. A tag like `v1.0.0` publishes `1.0.0`, which is the version your `devcontainer.json` will pin.

### Exercise 3

Commit and push. Then, in the bash Terminal, run `gh run list --limit 1`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: your-starter-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Commit and push. Then, in the bash Terminal, run gh run list --limit 1. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
your-starter $ gh run list --limit 1
*  Add Dockerfile and build workflow  build-and-push  main  push  31812345678  1m2s  1m
```

###

The `*` means it is still running. The first build is slow --- five minutes or so --- because the runner has to download the ~4 GB Rocker base image before it can add your one package. Re-run the command until the leading symbol turns into a `✓`. If it ever turns into an `X`, click through to the Actions tab on github.com: the log names the exact step that failed, and the cause is almost always a typo in one of the two files you just wrote.

### Exercise 4

Once the build is green, publish a versioned image by creating a release. In the bash Terminal, run `gh release create v1.0.0 --title "v1.0.0" --notes "First image."`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: your-starter-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Once the build is green, publish a versioned image by creating a release. In the bash Terminal, run gh release create v1.0.0 --title \"v1.0.0\" --notes \"First image.\". CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
your-starter $ gh release create v1.0.0 --title "v1.0.0" --notes "First image."
https://github.com/ppbds-student/your-starter/releases/tag/v1.0.0
```

###

Creating the release pushes a git tag `v1.0.0`. That matches the workflow's `tags: ['v*']` trigger and starts a second build, whose `type=semver` rule names the result `1.0.0`. This is the same release step PPBDS performs for every image version. `gh run list --limit 2` shows both builds. Wait for the second `✓`.

### Exercise 6

Now the file that ties it together. Create `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` with this content, again **replacing `YOUR_USERNAME` with your lowercase GitHub username**:

```json
{
  "name": "your-starter",
  "image": "ghcr.io/YOUR_USERNAME/your-starter:1.0.0",
  "customizations": {
    "vscode": {
      "extensions": [
        "reditorsupport.r@2.8.8"
      ],
      "settings": {
        "r.plot.useHttpgd": true,
        "files.autoSave": "afterDelay",
        "editor.wordWrap": "on"
      }
    }
  },
  "postAttachCommand": "echo 'your-starter is ready'"
}
```

Run `cat .devcontainer/devcontainer.json`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: your-starter-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Now the file that ties it together. Create .devcontainer/devcontainer.json with this content, again replacing YOUR_USERNAME with your lowercase GitHub username: name your-starter; image ghcr.io/YOUR_USERNAME/your-starter:1.0.0; under customizations, vscode, the extension reditorsupport.r@2.8.8 and the settings r.plot.useHttpgd true, files.autoSave afterDelay, and editor.wordWrap on; and postAttachCommand echo 'your-starter is ready'. Run cat .devcontainer/devcontainer.json. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
your-starter $ cat .devcontainer/devcontainer.json
{
  "name": "your-starter",
  "image": "ghcr.io/ppbds-student/your-starter:1.0.0",
```

###

`"image"` pins **your** image at an exact version, never `latest`. A floating tag would change your environment without you deciding it should. The R extension is pinned at `@2.8.8` for the same reason. `r.plot.useHttpgd` works because the Rocker base already includes `httpgd`. `files.autoSave` and `editor.wordWrap` are the two beginner-protection settings. `postAttachCommand` is the simplest possible ready signal, a one-line `echo` in place of `welcome.sh`.

### Exercise 7

Commit and push. Then run `git log --oneline -n 3`. CP/CR.

```{r}

  type = "reflection",

```

###

```{.output}
your-starter $ git log --oneline -n 3
a1b2c3d Add devcontainer.json
e4f5a6b Add Dockerfile and build workflow
0f1e2d3 Initial commit
```

###

The three commits are the three layers: what the image contains, how it gets built, and how a Codespace uses it. This push triggered one more `latest` build. It is harmless, since `devcontainer.json` is not part of the image and nothing in the Dockerfile changed.

### Exercise 8

On github.com, open your `your-starter` repo, click the green **Code** button, choose the **Codespaces** tab, and click **Create codespace on main**. It will take several minutes: your repo has no prebuild, so the container is built from scratch, pulling your image from GHCR. When the terminal appears, a line should print. Copy and paste it.

```{r}
#| label: your-starter-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "On github.com, open your your-starter repo, click the green Code button, choose the Codespaces tab, and click Create codespace on main. It will take several minutes: your repo has no prebuild, so the container is built from scratch, pulling your image from GHCR. When the terminal appears, a line should print. Copy and paste it.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
your-starter is ready
```

###

That line came from your `postAttachCommand`, which means the whole chain held: GitHub read your `devcontainer.json`, pulled `ghcr.io/…/your-starter:1.0.0` from the registry, started it, attached the editor, and ran your command. The slow start is what `codespace-starter` avoids with a prebuild (Settings → Codespaces on github.com). A prebuild costs storage, so leave it off until you use this starter often.

Back in your original Codespace, make `your-starter` a template. On github.com, open the repo's **Settings**, and near the top of **General**, check **Template repository**. Then, in the bash Terminal, run `gh repo view your-starter --json isTemplate`. CP/CR.

###

```{.output}
your-starter $ gh repo view your-starter --json isTemplate
{"isTemplate":true}
```

###

A template repo gains a green **Use this template** button. Each project you start that way gets its own repo, owned by you, that inherits `.devcontainer/`, so launching a Codespace from any of them gives you your environment. That also retires `connect-repo`. That script exists only because students launch from a repo they do not own.

Run `gh release list`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: your-starter-12
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run gh release list. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
```

```{.output}
your-starter $ gh release list
TITLE   TYPE    TAG NAME  PUBLISHED
v1.0.0  Latest  v1.0.0    about 20 minutes ago
```

###

The release is the durable record of what you published, and every future change runs through it: edit the Dockerfile, push, `gh release create v1.0.1`, wait for the build, change the `1.0.0` in your `devcontainer.json` to `1.0.1`, push again. The test Codespace you launched in Exercise 8 is still running. Go to https://github.com/codespaces, find the one on `your-starter`, and stop or delete it. You will start fresh ones from your template projects.

## Summary

You built the entire chain you spent three tutorials reading. A Dockerfile adds one package to a pinned base and tests it. A GitHub Actions workflow builds and publishes the image on every push and every `v*` release, tagged by pattern and logged in with a token no human handles. A `devcontainer.json` pins the published image at an exact version and configures the editor. A Codespace launched from all of it has your package inside. Turning the repo into a template makes it your `codespace-starter` from here on. To change the environment, edit the Dockerfile, push, release `v1.0.1`, and repin. That is the same loop PPBDS runs for every version you have used in this course.
